subject: Spanska
title: Articles and gender
sourceSummary: Definite and indefinite articles, gender (masculine/feminine), and the plural of nouns.

questions.prompt: Which gender do most words ending in -o have, like "libro" (book)?
questions.opener: -o and -a are the most common gender endings in Spanish.
choices: It never depends on the ending
questions.explanation: Words ending in -o are usually masculine, like "el libro" (the book). Words ending in -a are usually feminine, like "la mesa" (the table). Spanish has no neuter gender for nouns.

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "___ casa es grande." (The house is big.)
questions.opener: "Casa" ends in -a, a common feminine pattern.
questions.explanation: "Casa" is feminine and singular, so the article is "la". "El" is used for masculine words, "los"/"las" are plural.

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "___ chicos juegan en el parque." (The boys are playing in the park.)
questions.explanation: "Chicos" (boys) is masculine plural, so "los" is used. "Las" would be used for feminine plural, e.g. "las chicas".

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "Quiero comprar ___ manzana." (I want to buy an apple.)
questions.opener: "Manzana" is feminine singular — compare with "la manzana".
questions.explanation: "Una" is the indefinite article for feminine singular ("a/an"). "Un" is masculine, and "unos"/"unas" mean "some".

questions.prompt: What is the plural of "el profesor" (the teacher, male)?
questions.opener: Words ending in a consonant get the plural ending -es.
questions.explanation: Words ending in a consonant form the plural with -es: "profesor" → "profesores". The article also becomes "los" (masculine plural).

questions.prompt: Write the plural of "la mesa" (the table) — just the word for "table", not the article.
questions.opener: Words ending in a vowel only get an -s in the plural.

questions.prompt: Correct the two errors: "El mesa es nueva y tengo un manzana roja."
questions.opener: Check the gender of "mesa" and "manzana" — both end in -a.
questions.answer: La mesa es nueva y tengo una manzana roja.
steps: "El mesa" → "La mesa". "Mesa" (table) is feminine, so the article should be "la", not "el".
"Un manzana" → "una manzana". "Manzana" (apple) is also feminine, so it should be "una", not "un".
Remember the rule of thumb: words ending in -a are usually feminine and take la/una, words ending in -o are usually masculine and take el/un.

questions.prompt: How do gender, definite/indefinite articles, and the plural work in Spanish?
questions.opener: The basic rules for -o/-a and how the articles follow along.
questions.answer: Gender: words in -o are usually masculine (el libro), words in -a are usually feminine (la mesa) — but there are exceptions to learn separately, like "el día" (the day) and "la mano" (the hand). Definite article: el (masc. sg.), la (fem. sg.), los (masc. pl.), las (fem. pl.). Indefinite article: un (masc. sg.), una (fem. sg.), unos (masc. pl., 'some'), unas (fem. pl., 'some'). Plural: vowel + -s (mesa → mesas), consonant + -es (profesor → profesores).

questions.prompt: Which of these words is a common exception that is feminine despite ending in -o?
questions.opener: This word means "the hand" and is a classic exception to the -o/-a rule.
questions.explanation: "La mano" (the hand) is feminine despite ending in -o — one of the most important exceptions to memorize. "El día" is the corresponding exception in the other direction (masculine despite -a).

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "___ agua está fría." (The water is cold.)
questions.opener: "Agua" is actually feminine, but starts with a stressed a-sound, which changes which article form is used in the singular.
questions.explanation: Feminine words that start with a stressed a-/ha- sound, like "agua", use "el" in the singular for pronunciation reasons (to avoid two a-sounds in a row), even though the word is still feminine — which is why it's "el agua fría", not "el agua frío".

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "Tengo ___ perro y ___ gata." (I have a dog and a cat.)
questions.explanation: "Un" is used for masculine words like "perro" (dog) and "una" for feminine words like "gata" (female cat).

questions.prompt: What is the plural of "la ciudad" (the city)?
questions.explanation: Words ending in a consonant form the plural with -es: "ciudad" → "ciudades". The article also becomes "las" (feminine plural).

questions.prompt: What is the plural of "el lápiz" (the pencil)?
questions.opener: Words ending in -z usually swap the z for c in the plural.
questions.explanation: Words ending in -z change to -ces in the plural: "lápiz" → "lápices". This is a common spelling rule in Spanish.

questions.prompt: What gender is the word "la clase" (the class/lesson)?
questions.opener: The word ends in -e, which doesn't always reveal gender directly.
questions.explanation: "Clase" is feminine: "la clase". Words ending in -e can be either masculine or feminine and often have to be learned individually.

questions.prompt: Choose the right article: "___ estudiantes llegan tarde." (The students are arriving late.)
questions.opener: A mixed or unspecified group of students takes the masculine article in standard Spanish.
questions.explanation: "Los estudiantes" is used for a group of students, regardless of gender, following the traditional rule that masculine plural is used for mixed groups.
